beats.narration: Hold out your wrist and look at the veins. About five litres of blood are looping through you right now, completing a full round trip of your body in under a minute. But blood isn't just a red liquid — it's a fleet of four different workers. Let's meet them.
Here's the whole team. Plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Four components, four completely different jobs. Watch each one carefully.

Plasma is the liquid itself — it carries digested food, carbon dioxide, and wastes, all dissolved in it. Red cells are the oxygen couriers: they're packed with haemoglobin, an iron-rich pigment that grabs oxygen in the lungs. That iron is why blood is red.

White cells are the army — the moment an infection enters, they hunt it down and destroy it. Platelets are the repair crew: cut your finger, and within minutes they clot the leak and seal it. Without them, even a small cut would never stop bleeding.

Now, the roads this fleet travels on. Arteries carry blood away from the heart — thick-walled, because the pressure is high. Veins bring it back — thinner walls, and fitted with valves so the slow-moving blood can't slip backwards. Between them, capillaries so thin that only one cell passes at a time.

One line to keep: plasma carries, red cells deliver oxygen, white cells defend, platelets repair — and arteries go away from the heart while veins return to it. Exams love the artery-versus-vein difference. Anything unclear, raise your hand.
